utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've asked for the witness to be kept out. I have a short matter to raise that has absolutely nothing to do with his evidence. It relates to the decision on the admission of documents in connection with the testimony of Defence witness Dragan Jasovic, which was filed last Friday and about which we obviously have to give consideration. I'd be very grateful for, as it were, clarification of one issue. I can either put it in the question form, which would be inappropriate, or put it in the issue form, which might be appropriate. The issue is this: Whether admissibility or, rather, admission of the Jasovic Defence material is effective for all purposes and for all time or whether if the Prosecution Jasovic material is admitted into evidence at the rebuttal stage of the case, the issue of the admissibility of Jasovic's material is still open for consideration or whether at that stage the Prosecution Jasovic material, if admitted into evidence, would only go to issues of fact and weight and credibility. Now, that's the issue. As I say, I don't want to -- it's not for me to raise it in the form of a question. It may be that the Chamber will say that the decision is clear on its face. It may be that it would be able to assist us by saying, yes, it's admitted for all purposes and for all time and Prosecution material in respect of Jasovic would only ever go to weight, fact, and credibility. I don't know if the Chamber would be able to assist us sometime today. We would be grateful if so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I must give you what is my personal view on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I do not think it is proper to utilise the Court's time to raise issues of law of that -- of that nature. The Chamber has given its decision, and you must live with the decision. If matters arise, then we'll deal with them, but this habit of the Prosecution attempting to reopen matters that have been decided by the Chamber is something that must stop, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not ascribing ill motives to you, but the Chamber has made its decision and, in my view, the decision is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would certainly be entirely, if I may say so, absolutely inappropriate to ascribe bad motives. This is an attempt to clarify issues in our own mind so that we can take our appropriate, if any, next step. If the Chamber feels it can't assist me, then I shall obviously act accordingly. If it feels it can, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ex abundanti cautela. What I say is that we take note of what you have said, and if we find it appropriate, we'll respond. Please call the witness. Mr. Nice, I might say that we did consider that matter, and in our view it's admissible for all purposes. The question of weight is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful and I'm actually much assisted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We left off yesterday just before paragraph -- or at paragraph 36 of the Croatian indictment. That's on page 9. Could you please find that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to deal with the preceding part dealing with persecutions, and then comes paragraph 36 that is rather extensive. It says that "persecutions were based on political, racial, or religious grounds and included the following..." Then it goes on to talk about "the extermination or murder of hundreds of Croat and other non-Serb civilians in Dalj, Erdut, Klisa, Lovas, Vukovar, Vocin, Bacin, Saborsko and neighbouring villages, Skabrnja, Nadin, Bruska, and Dubrovnik and its environs, as described in detail in paragraphs 38 to 59 and 73 to 75." Tell me, please, Mr. Seselj, all these references here, do they have anything to do with Serbia or any authorities in Serbia, without going into what really happened or didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some of these places, crimes indeed happened. In some of those -- in some other places, there were no crimes. For instance, in Dubrovnik there was not a single crime against the civilian population. In the course of the operations to capture Dubrovnik, there was a murder in a village in Herzegovina of certain villagers. It's the village called Kijev Do on the Bobanska plateau, but the man who perpetrated these crimes was a soldier of the JNA, a reservist from Montenegro, as far as I remember, and he was convicted to ten years in prison by the competent military court. On the territory of the municipality of Dubrovnik itself, there were no killings of civilians. As for the departure of civilians from many places, that was organised by the Croatian authorities before the JNA arrived. In some other places enumerated here, crimes indeed happened but Serbia could not have been involved in any way because it was mainly JNA that was active in those areas, and why some of these crimes were never investigated or prosecuted is something that the Trial Chamber could find out from Aleksandar Vasiljevic, chief of the military security, because for all these crimes it was the competent military courts that were in charge. Civilian courts in Belgrade could not prosecute these crimes then, but the civilian court in Belgrade is prosecuting currently some of those crimes. But in fact it is military courts that are in charge for any crimes perpetrated by members of the armed forces and war crimes. Our legislation stipulated very precisely the prosecution of any crimes that fall under the Geneva Conventions, various international treaties and covenants, and in the legislation of the former Yugoslavia, that was stipulated in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, did the authorities in Serbia, including any agency of the government or myself as president of the republic, did they have any capacity whatsoever to gain insight into what was going on in some of those places that are enumerated here at the time when the SFRY existed and institutions functioned?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no institutional capacity to find out or again this information. There was only hearsay, unreliable reports from the media, et cetera, but there were no institutional channels. Only the federal authorities had such institutional channels or, rather, the authorities of the JNA, through military courts and the state -- or, rather, the security service of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at this reference to Serbia in the following subsection of the same paragraph 36. That's subparagraph (b), which refers to "prolonged and routine imprisonment and confinement of thousands of Croat and other non-Serb civilians in detention facilities within and outside of Croatia..." I'm not going to deal with this bit about Croatia, because that has nothing to do with Serbia whatsoever. But it also says, "prison camps located in Montenegro, Serbia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina -" so Serbia is one of these places - "as described in detail in paragraph 64." And now if you turn to page 16 of this same document, you will see what paragraph 64 says. So (d), (e), (f) and (g), as far as I could make out. These subparagraphs contain allegations that served as a basis for many charges here. Look at what it says: (d) -- paragraph 64, subparagraph (d). I think you've found it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Stajicevo agricultural farm in Serbia... approximately 1.700 detainees. "(e) military barracks in Begejci in Serbia run by the JNA, approximately 260 detainees. "(f) military barracks in Zrenjanin in Serbia run by the JNA, scores of detainees. "(g) military prison Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia run by the JNA, hundreds of detainees." Now, please answer this: Since Serbia is mentioned in all of these subparagraphs, and I hope I haven't omitted anything, and it refers to facilities run by the JNA, did Serbia have any competencies there? Did Serbian authorities have any powers over these affairs that were dealt with by JNA agencies? But also tell me, what is this about in the first place?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say emphatically that the authorities in Serbia could have absolutely no powers or competencies in these places because all of them were JNA facilities, JNA installations. I never even heard about these installations in Stajicevo, Begejci and Zrenjanin where somebody was detained, but I know about the military prison in Sremska Mitrovica. However, the JNA could bring only prisoners of war to these places. I don't know that a single civilian was among them. A civilian could have been arrested - a civilian, a person who wasn't wearing a uniform. Such a person could have been captured if they nevertheless took part in combat on the side of Croatian armed forces, paramilitaries, et cetera. But a very small number, if any, were tried. They were all of them released quite simply without any charges and they were able to travel wherever they wanted. I think most of them opted for Croatia. To the best of my knowledge, in the military facilities where detainees were kept, there was not a single murder or killing. And that includes facilities in Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the JNA placed some prisoners of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro facilities while they were fighting Croatian separatists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at this. The conflict was going in Croatia with those attacks on military barracks that were going on, and the conflict was between the existing federal army and the Croatian national forces, and some prisoners were taken in the process, and this is all ascribed to the authorities in Serbia. Could that be true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian authorities could have had nothing to do with it. They had no powers or competencies and they had no effective involvement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look now at the paragraph 66. It says: "By these acts and omissions, Slobodan Milosevic committed ..." That is to say the fact that the JNA took some prisoners of war in the conflicts in another territory, I committed - look at this - imprisonment, a crime against humanity; torture, a crime against humanity; inhumane acts, a crime against humanity; unlawful confinement; torture again; wilfully causing great suffering; cruel treatment, and so on. First of all, to the best your knowledge, did the JNA torture anybody of these camps or prisons?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All JNA authorities had strict instructions to act in consistence with their regulations. I don't know if there have been any incidents - I haven't heard about any - but I know for a fact there hadn't been any killings. The JNA had its own general enactments and bylaws and rules of procedure and regulations that stipulated precisely how prisoners of war were to be treated. All of these were written in conformity with international rules. There is a reference here to the violation of the Geneva Conventions. That could not be true because there were no international conflicts. Violations of the additional Protocol B could have occurred because what was going on was a civil war, but it is absolutely nonsensical that you could be responsible for anything that happened, imprisonment, torture, inhumane acts, unlawful confinement and wilful causing of great suffering, et cetera. You could have had no involvement or role in that. And I would also like to draw your attention to another thing. In addition to the JNA, some other players are being mentioned here that could not have been under the JNA control at all times. And then a general conclusion is drawn from all this -- or, rather, an inference. Lovas, for instance, Dusan Silni units, Arkan's men, et cetera. A distinction has to be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking now about places of confinement or places of detention outside of Serbia. References to Serbia relate only to military Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. facilities run by the JNA, and the JNA as a federal institution is the only one who was in charge, whereas the Republic of Serbia did not have any authority over it. Were Serbian authorities able to enter any of these facilities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at subparagraph (k) of paragraph 36. I am charged with the deportation or forcible transfer of at least 170.000 Croats and other non-Serb civilians from the territories specified above, I'm not going to enumerate them now, and then it refers to their deportation to Serbia. Who was it who deported Croats to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think it's pure fabrication. I never heard of a single Croat civilian deported to Serbia ever. But there are some other things that are completely made up here. For instance, in Ilok there were no combat actions at all, but most civilians still wanted to move out of Ilok, and the media covered it widely at the time. And as far as I remember, there were no armed operations in Ilok at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at what they refer to in connection with this subparagraph (k). They invoke details described in paragraphs 67 to 69. So look at 67. It reads: "From the 1st of August, 1991, until May 1992," and that is the period about which they themselves say that the SFRY existed then. So they go on to say, "Slobodan Milosevic, acting alone or in concert with other known and unknown members of the joint criminal enterprise, planned, instigated, ordered, committed," et cetera, et cetera, "aided and abetted the deportations or forcible transfers of the Croat and other non-Serb civilian populations." That is all in -- during the existence of the SFRY. And then paragraph 68: "In order to achieve this objective, Serb forces comprised of JNA, TO and volunteer units including the 'White Eagles,' 'Seselj's men' -" so this is a specific reference to your name - "'Dusan Silni' and 'Arkan's Tigers,' in cooperation with police units, including 'Martic's Police,' SNB -" I don't know what that means but it is probably again -- I don't know what SNB means - "and Serbian MUP and others under the effective control of Slobodan Milosevic or other participants in the joint criminal enterprise, surrounded Croat towns and villages and demanded their inhabitants to surrender their weapons, including legally owned hunting rifles. Then, the towns and villages were attacked, even when those inhabitants had complied with the demands. These attacks were intended to compel the population to flee." And then it goes on to say that they were "... forcibly transferred to locations in Croatia controlled by the Croatian government or deported to locations outside Croatia, in particular Serbia and Montenegro." Mr. Seselj, what can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was never any plan about the deportation or forcible transfer of the Croatian or any other population. Secondly, there was never an organised or systematic deportation or forcible transfer. Thirdly, there is not a single case where Croats who had previously been armed by the Tudjman regime handed over their weapons to the JNA or to the Territorial Defence or the Serbian police and after that hand-over their villages were attacked. There is no such case, not a single one. Tudjman armed the Croats intensively in areas where the Serb population was in the majority, in the Krajina, and there is evidence to support this. I've already mentioned a case where weapons were found in shipments of flour for the Croats in Knin. The Serbian authorities of the Krajina and the JNA demanded the handing over of those weapons, but nowhere where weapons were actually handed over was there an attack. Such things happened only in Bosnia where, in the village of Glogova, the Muslims handed over their weapons after which 65 helpless civilians were slaughtered and killed. In the conflicts on the former Croatian federal unit, this never happened. And finally, even had this happened, you could not have had any role in it whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, not to speak only of my own role. Could the authorities of the Republic of Serbia or the representatives of its government have had a role?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. There was no organ of the Republic of Serbia who had any kind of competencies there. Only volunteers from Serbia could have been there as part of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. No official players from Serbia could have been present on the ground there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Seselj, the question and the answer appear to proceed on the basis of what was the de jure position. You just said that Serbia had no competence in that area, but I have to remind you that the indictment proceeds on the basis that there were laws, there were legal competencies assigned, but these were breached. So it's not an answer to the indictment simply to say what the de jure position was. You will see references to effective control. What the indictment is looking at is what happened as a matter of fact before the laws were complied with. Then there would have been no indictment, for the essential allegation in the indictment is that there were laws and legal competencies properly assigned to certain organs but these were breached, and it is the breaches which happened as a matter of fact that the indictment alleges. So I'd invite you to attend to the factual situation, to answer the factual situation. So in addition to saying what the legal position is, then you should also say, if that is your evidence - I cannot say whether it is your evidence - that nothing of that kind happened as matter of fact, and then I think you would be giving what might be a more complete answer to the allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, on a separate matter, who was responsible for killing the 65 Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miroslav Deronjic. Miroslav Deronjic demanded -- he was the president of the Crisis Staff of Bratunac municipality, and he demanded that the Muslims hand over their weapons and guaranteed full security for them if they did. They handed over their weapons and then Deronjic attacked the village of Glogova and 65 unarmed Muslim civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand, Mr. Robinson, what you are talking about, but I assert that de facto no institution and no government body in Serbia took part in breaches of the law on the territory of the Krajina. In those places where there was sporadic breaches of the law -- and these figures here are exaggerated, there's no doubt of it. It's not possible that 170.000 Croats were deported. The Croats mostly left of their own accord, just as the Serbs fled from the territories under the control of the Serb forces. Likewise, the same happened on this side. And of course there were breaches of the law in places, but de facto no official body from Serbia was involved in such breaches of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbia cannot be held responsible for something that Arkan's Tigers may have done, Dusan Silni, the White Eagles, and so on. That has nothing to do with the government authorities in Serbia. That's my testimony. Neither formally nor de facto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, now that we're discussing this topic - let's leave these quotations aside for a moment - at the time of these civil wars in Croatia and Bosnia, from 1991 until the end of the war, did any Croats or Muslims whose forces were fighting the Serb forces in Croatia and Bosnia, were any of these people expelled from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one was ever forcibly removed or expelled or deported from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone arrested in Serbia because of their ethnicity or discriminated in any way throughout these ten years?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee that in Serbia throughout all this time no one was ever arrested because of their ethnic, racial, or religious affiliation, and no one was discriminated against in any way as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you remember that in Serbia we had Muslim refugees from Bosnia? There were over 70.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of Muslims from the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina took refuge in Serbia when war broke out, especially those who had relatives or friends or who were able to find their way to Serbia in some other way. And those who did not were assisted by the authorities in Serbia in the same way that the Serbs who had been expelled or who had fled were assisted. No distinction was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a single case of someone arriving in Serbia, which was completely peaceful and where there was no fighting, no war, who did not receive protection, who was not able to live in peace like any other citizen?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is not a single instance of anything like that. Let me draw your attention to a characteristic example. During the operations for the liberation of Srebrenica in 1995, a large number -- I can't be precise about the number, but a large number of Muslim soldiers swam across the River Drina and fled to Serbia. In Serbia, they were given decent accommodation, and a few days later they were allowed to leave and go wherever they wanted. It never occurred to anyone to hand them over to the Serb authorities of Republika Srpska. It never occurred to anyone to hand them over to Miroslav Deronjic in Bratunac, for example. They could leave Serbia and go literally wherever they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was an entire brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number of men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the following day, they were visited by all the diplomatic representatives at my request.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for certain that they were given decent accommodation, that they were given decent food while they were accommodated there. Nobody ever maltreated them and they were able to leave and go literally wherever they liked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it says here that I, because this is an indictment against me, but also the authorities of Serbia deported people and that I thereby committed deportation, a crime against humanity, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions, and so on. In view of the fact that this trial is public, the citizens of Serbia who witnessed what was happening in Serbia all this time should hear what the charges against me are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The indictment is public.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, people can't read this on the Internet, citizens, but a large number of people in Serbia and Republika Srpska is following this on television, and they're all amazed at what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that remark because the trial is not to be used for that purpose, to publicise the indictment. It's already public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Seselj, in paragraph (l), and this is something I am charged with, it says here, "wilful destruction of residential housing and other public and historical --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking for a fuller reference. 36(l). I think he just said (l). 36(l).

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 36 (l). As I'm dealing with 36, I thought they would bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look here: "The deliberate destruction of homes, other public and private property," and so on and so forth, "of the non-Serb population in Dubrovnik and its environs, Vukovar, Erdut, Lovas, Sarengrad, Bapska, Tovarnik, Vocin, Saborsko, Skabrnja, Nadin and Bruska, as described," it says here, "in paragraphs 71 and 77 to 82." Let us now look at paragraph 71, where this is described. It says that this is wanton destruction, plunder of public or private property. So I wantonly destroyed and plundered public or private property. "From the 1st of August 1991 until May 1992, Slobodan Milosevic, acting alone or in concert with other known and unknown members of the joint criminal enterprise, planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation, or execution of the wanton destruction and plunder of the public and private property of the Croat and other non-Serb population, within the territories of the SAO SBWS ... although these actions were not justified by military necessity." What kind of military force from Serbia was in that area? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no armed force from Serbia active in these areas. It was exclusively the JNA. Sporadically certain paramilitary formations who were outside JNA control did turn up, and there was looting and deliberate destruction but never under orders from the JNA commands. These could only have been isolated incidents, groups turning up to loot. That did occur. But these groups that engaged in looting could have had nothing to do with the government authorities in Serbia either formally or de facto.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's very clear because -- it's very important that you always draw attention to the de facto situation as Mr. Robinson has this aspect in mind.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looting was a frequent occurrence on both sides. That cannot be denied. It did happen, but this was never organised or systematically carried out by the Serb side, either by the government organs of Serbian Krajina or by the JNA. This was done by spontaneously organised gangs of robbers and looters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here from the 1st of August, and this refers to Dalj, Vukovar, Erdut, Lovas, Sarengrad, Bapska and Tovarnik from August to October 1992; and then Western Slavonia from August to December 1991, SAO Krajina from August to December 1991, and these towns are listed again. Tell me, those periods of time from August to October to December 1991, who was participating in the hostilities at the time throughout this period in all these locations?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the JNA with the Croatian separatist paramilitary formations throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it says here that at that time, from August to October 1991 during the conflicts in Croatia I committed widespread plunder and destruction not justified by military necessity, that I wantonly destroyed and plundered villages, destroyed and -- intentionally destroyed homes and religious and cultural buildings. When it says here religious and cultural buildings, Mr. Seselj, throughout these events was a single mosque or Catholic church destroyed in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Serbia not a single mosque or Catholic church was destroyed, or any other house of worship. However, in some of these places, such as Vukovar, for example, I know of no building that was destroyed deliberately, either privately owned or religious or any other. Large numbers of buildings were destroyed during the military operations. Even the Orthodox church in Vukovar has been destroyed. I know of no building in Vukovar that was destroyed intentionally, targeted by someone because it was a certain kind of building. But in Vukovar, literally there was fighting for every house, for every building. One could say that the JNA did not have a well developed tactics of taking part in urban warfare, which is why they lost quite a large number of tanks initially and so on. But literally there was fighting for every building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When we are talking about Vukovar, it's a very important subject here anyway, how did these conflicts come about in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts in Vukovar came about because the Croatian paramilitary forces surrounded the JNA barracks and started targeting it from different weapons. Secondly, in the area of Vukovar, the Croatian police and paramilitary forces tried to threaten the Serb civilian population. Before the war, it cannot be said that there was any majority population in Vukovar among all the ethnic groups. However, the Serbs were rather numerous. That numerous that even the mayor of Vukovar was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you in Vukovar at the time? Were you in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. During the war I was in Vukovar twice, and I was there once before the war, too, sometime in the spring of 1991. That's when it was very calm and peaceful in Vukovar. I freely walked about the streets of Vukovar in civilian clothing without any kind of armed escorts, and there were no incidents whatsoever. During the war, I came twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But were you there at the relevant time in relation to the conflicts alleged in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Twice during the relevant time. The last time was a month or 20 days prior to the liberation of Vukovar. The first time was about a month before the liberation of Vukovar. It's hard to remember the exact dates but it's not hard to establish them. I always went to the front line, and I saw with my very own eyes that there was fighting literally going on for every house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I ask the question because your evidence is so wide-ranging. Mr. Milosevic, it might be as well if you elicited from the witness the basis for his knowledge in relation to this very wide range of matters that he's testifying about. It will help to make his evidence more credible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my understanding that the witness had presented the basis for his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, please, have you got anything to add to this? You were there on the spot itself. You had your own volunteers within the Yugoslav People's Army. You communicated with citizens. You communicated with officials at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Milosevic. You must ask the witness the question. You're giving him the answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the question. Well, I'm asking. He's already enumerated all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all these persons, are they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at this. It says here in subparagraph (l) -- I've already read out 71 to you and you commented on it, and then from 77 to 82, it says. Look at 77 to 82. It's an entire page, everything contained in this indictment against me.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's Dubrovnik, as far as I can see. And then it says here from the 1st of October, 1991, until the 7th of December, 1991. Look at that. It seems that I waged some kind of artillery warfare here. It says that Slobodan Milosevic -- that: "... during this same shelling attack, Slobodan Milosevic, acting alone or in concert with other known and unknown members of the joint criminal enterprise --" perhaps I shouldn't read all of this since it's the usual thing -- "planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation and execution of the wanton destruction or wilful damage and plunder of the public and private property of the Croat and other non-Serb population within the area of the Dubrovnik Republic." Please, Mr. Seselj, was there anyone from Serbia in the territory of the Dubrovnik Republic in any way; directly, indirectly, whatever?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, only I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was my understanding that you were there to tour the Herzegovina front.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was in the area of Konavle while the fighting was going on. I visited some JNA units. One day I was there where the actual firing squad of a unit was. I saw with my very own eyes that in Konavle not a single house had been destroyed or looted. There were a few cases when I saw some cows that were killed by crossfire lying by the road, three or four cows. Not a single house was destroyed or damaged. The soldiers had strict orders not to touch civilian property. However, when the JNA was withdrawing towards the end of 1991, then there was some spontaneous looting. Probably it was hard for anyone to keep the soldiers under control then, and that is when people broke into private homes and looted property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just get this clear. Who was it that was looting this property in Konavle? Was it soldiers from Serbia, reservists, active duty soldiers? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was doing this in Konavle?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, only reservists from Montenegro were there. Recently Milo Djukanovic admitted that some livestock had been stolen in Konavle and taken to Montenegro and now he paid whatever, 300.000 euro by way of damages, but nothing came to Serbia. None of this came to Serbia. Also, as regards the shelling of the old town, that happened sometime in the first half of December, because from the old town the Croatian paramilitary forces opened fire at JNA units. JNA units had casualties, fatalities from the gunfire, and then fire was returned. According to international law, the very instant someone abuses a place of worship or any cultural monument as a place for engaging in armed activity, from that moment onwards, such a facility is no longer protected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let's just get this clear. This is what paragraph 81 says. I'm just going to read the beginning out to you. It says: "In October 1991, the Serb forces took control of the Croatian towns and villages Konavle, Zupa Dubrovacka --"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where's that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, in all these operations around Dubrovnik, in everything that happened around Dubrovnik, can this term be used at all, this term "Serb"? What kind of Serb forces took control of Dubrovnik? So what is written here, "Serb forces," were there any Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a single member of any Serb forces in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no Serb forces there. There were only units of the JNA, only units of the JNA. There weren't any paramilitary forces either or Territorial Defence. In Trebinje, truth to tell, there was a TO unit that was mobilised, but it didn't take part in the operations at all. It was only operations units of the JNA that were taking part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then reference is made here to all sorts of localities; Dubrovnik, various places around Dubrovnik, the area of Dubrovacka Zupa and so on. Do you know that at that time the minister of defence, Veljko Kadijevic, told all of us that it was not true at all that the army was engaged in any operations in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The newspapers were full of reports to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Do you know at that time the minister of defence, Veljko Kadijevic, told all of us ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic: Not permissible form of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And once more on an absolutely critical issue. So the whole issue is now valueless from the mouth of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, since you're on your feet, in paragraph 77 of the indictment there's a reference to the area of the Dubrovnik Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that a proper reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure it's a proper reference. Let me see how -- I'll get an answer for why it was used, if that would help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But may I come back to that a little bit later because I think that, given the history of the drafting of these documents, which goes back over several years, it would be preferable for me to get you a concise and simple answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, were you in the area of Dubrovnik at all during the month of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My knowledge about what was going on in the month of December is indirect, but I was in Dubrovnik sometime in the end of September or beginning of October 1991, when the operations in Konavle were going on. I was in Konavle while the fighting was still going on. I was in Popovo Polje. I was in some other localities. I went all the way up to Ljubinje. That's where the front line was, at Cavaska Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Gradina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. And no leading questions, particularly on matters that are at issue between the Prosecution and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, at that time -- or generally speaking, did Serbia have any forces that it could have sent to Dubrovnik even if it wanted to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Serbia did not have a military force or police unit that it could have sent to the Dubrovnik front line even if it had wanted to. It did not have any such thing. Also, in connection with this mention of the Dubrovnik Republic, there was an initiative by an opposition party in Montenegro to re-establish this republic. However, this initiative was never carried through. That is the historical area of the Dubrovnik Republic, but this Dubrovnik Republic was abolished by Napoleon in 1808. After Napoleon's defeat, it became part of Austro-Hungary or, rather, Austria, and all the way up to 1918 it was within Austria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, if you look at all the counts mentioned here as we are dealing with them in order, is there a grain of truth in anything that is written here in this alleged indictment of Mr. Nice's?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But what I find of particular interest is that this indictment was issued in Zagreb. I assume that indictments before this Tribunal are issued in The Hague. This is an exception, that an indictment against a Serb, the then president of the Republic of Serbia, was issued in Zagreb. In Zagreb, Croatia, the 23rd of October, 2002. It's all clear. It's all clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to deal with some of the other counts here, although it is quite clear, I believe, to anyone who wishes to read this or to hear this. Please look at paragraph 39 now. Again we see your name there, but I'm not asking you only because your name appears there, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, get on with the questions. This is not an occasion for comments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in order to put a question I have to indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just indicate the relevant paragraph and put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 39. I have it on page 11 in the Serbian text, although I honour this language used here by calling it Serbian, because it is really below any acceptable level. So it says here that "Beginning August 1991 the Serb forces including the volunteer units 'Seselj's men' and the 'White Eagles' were in control of Vocin. On the 13th of December 1991, while the Serb forces withdrew from Vocin and the surrounding area, they went from house to house, killing a substantial portion of the remaining Croat civilian population." So these two units are Seselj's men and the White Eagles. A total of 32 civilians were killed by these two units before they withdrew on the 13th of December, 1991. The names of the victims are set out in Annex 1, and so on. Do you know anything about this; and if so, can you tell us about this? Was there a volunteer unit of yours there in that area that could have carried out any kind of crime in the area?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there were no volunteer units that were Seselj's men. There were volunteers of the Serb Radical Party within the ranks of the JNA who, on orders from the command of the JNA in charge, were deployed in the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia and were placed under the control of the active army Colonel Trbojevic. Our volunteers had strict political orders from the Serb Radical Party not to have any contacts whatsoever with the White Eagles. I've already said that, to the best of my knowledge, Veljko Dzakula brought the White Eagles to Western Slavonia. How this happened can best be explained by General Aleksandar Vasiljevic. I did not take part in having them brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Who was Veljko Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Dzakula was the president of the Assembly of Western Slavonia. On one occasion he was arrested in Belgrade on the suspicion that he was a Croat spy, and he was kept in prison I don't know how many days. He was suspected of working for the Croatian intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what grounds?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was his conduct that gave rise to that suspicion. I don't remember all that very well but I remember the time when he was arrested and I remember why he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you just said, what is it based on, your claim that Veljko Dzakula was the one who brought White Eagles to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that already in 1991. When I was in Western Slavonia, I also avoided all contact with the White Eagles. I didn't meet with them at all. I met with many soldiers, with volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, with many civilians, both Serb and Croat, but I avoided categorically all contact with members of the White Eagles. They were, in my eyes, untouchables. And wherever they were, volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were told as a political suggestion, it was only a political suggestion that did not bind them in any way, they could only have been expelled from the party for non-compliance, but they had the political instruction not to contact with the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who controlled the White Eagles at the time? Who commanded them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Dzakula, as far as I know. Veljko Dzakula pursued his own policy that was distinct from the policy of the leadership of the Serbian Autonomous District of Western Slavonia. And all the time when I was in Western Slavonia, I met with Vukelic, Prime Minister, Mr. Sasic and other members of the leadership, but I never, ever met with Veljko Dzakula, because the policies diverged drastically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that your withdrew -- these units withdrew in December 1991. Were they still there at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And their withdrawal was rather chaotic when it happened because the Serb forces could not withstand the onslaught of Croatian paramilitary formations. On one day in the defence of Masicka Sagovina, many volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party got killed in one day and more were wounded. Many were taken prisoners. But I have no information whatsoever that anybody killed Croatian civilians while withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's just an allegation put in here by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it looks very nice here, the way it's put without any evidence to support it, but it's not difficult at all to establish who by name --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... comment in this way on matters that are not his province.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a little bit on the balance, Mr. Nice, as to whether the witness can say there is no evidence to support it. But, Mr. Seselj, avoid comments of that kind. That may be more a proper comment coming from the accused. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Seselj, in connection with what Mr. Nice just commented upon, I will ask you about something that is definitely your province; Seselj's men. Did any Seselj's men exist there as an armed unit, or is it true that there was a volunteer unit or is it simply a lie?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that an armed unit, Seselj's men, existed, and it often happened that -- that volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party and the unit they formed were referred to as Seselj's men. Locals called them Seselj's men, but there was no such thing as an armed unit officially called Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before moving on, the start of that answer was, "It is true that an armed unit, Seselj's men, existed ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know what your interpreters are doing. I didn't say that, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we -- it's of some importance, so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an error by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj is beginning to answer too quickly after the question is posed and that creates a lot of problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, here we have -- here we have come to the crux of the -- one of the major problems throughout your evidence. The blame for this difficulty is being placed squarely on your shoulders by answering far too quickly, and we have now an answer that appears to say it is true that an armed unit, Seselj's men, existed. Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't want this to happen, but I'm not to blame. I can't accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also the result of another problem in the presentation of this evidence, that this particular question has been asked over and over again and it's inevitable, I suppose, if you ask it long enough, you'll cause confusion -- rather, ask it often enough, you'll cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one thing is missing here, the word "not." The record currently says, "It is true," whereas Mr. Seselj said, "It is not true." That's what Mr. Seselj said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Seselj. You see the kind of problem that can arise by answering too quickly. Once again, you must observe a pause before answering Mr. Milosevic. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a pause. A long pause is necessary. You always start to answer while the translation of the question is being -- going on. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, even those volunteers who were at that time within the JNA, were they under your control?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In no way could they have been under my control. However, in a certain way I tried to make sure and made additional efforts to persuade them that they should be disciplined, but the only thing I would have -- I could have done to sanction any untoward behaviour was to expel them from the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any elements from Serbia in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no elements from Serbia in Western Slavonia, formally or informally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: De jure or de facto?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you know any -- anything about the events in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about these events. I even publicly condemned the perpetrators of these crimes. But since that came to fall within my indictment, I don't want to repeat who I condemned. The Office of the Prosecutor has in their possession all my public statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they charged you on account of your address to the volunteers in Vocin and thereby instigating the crimes that followed; the burning, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They can charge me with whatever they like. They can charge me for Kennedy's murder if they like. It's up to them. But it's a real delicacy for me to tear apart the indictment raised against me. I'm testifying here about your indictment and my knowledge about the events I have any knowledge of. The killing of a certain number of Croat civilians did occur. I don't know the exact number. As soon as I found out about it, I publicly condemned the perpetrators in Belgrade. And I know that General Vasiljevic, who happened to be in Western Slavonia during its fall, did not do anything. I'll give you another fact. One of the commanders of those units that included volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party was Radovan Novacic. Radovan Novacic's father is a Croat. It's not possible that Radovan Novacic, who was a true Yugoslav of truly Yugoslav orientation -- and he was close to Vocin, commanding a company, I think. He was at Vocin and I visited him too. He lost a lot during the war. It's not possible that Radovan Novacic would be killing Croat civilians if his father is a Croat. Father was a Croat and mother was Serbian. He wanted to preserve Croatia within Yugoslavia maybe, but not kill Croat civilians. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript on page 10.432, Witness C037 states that some local people told him that your radicals had taken part in causing the exodus of the population on the 23rd of December, 1991, in Pakrac. Have you got any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You know, this secondhand testimony is always unreliable. I'll give you a specific example. A story circulated or, rather, cropped up in various places in Bosnia and Herzegovina that Seselj was coming with thousands of his Chetniks. He was feeding them some pills whose effect was to keep them awake, able to go without sleep, for a week without eating. They can keep on cutting throats. That's one of the stories that circulated. I am here to talk about facts, not to discuss other people's fantasy. It's a big problem when you bring witnesses who testify about something that somebody told them. That's nonsense. No lawyer can treat this with any seriousness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I observe that you have given evidence of that kind, and the Chamber -- the Chamber receives it. We are allowed to receive hearsay evidence. The question as to what weight is to be attached to it is another matter. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really have the impression that Mr. Seselj was giving hearsay evidence, but we can establish that from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has given hearsay evidence in answer to Judge Bonomy as to whether he was in a particular place in, I think, December 1991. He said no, he wasn't there. How did he get the information? He received it. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another witness was Dzuro Matovina here. He was not a protected witness. His testimony is on page 10996, 7 December 2002. He mentions in his testimony that during attacks on Vocin and surrounding villages volunteers under your command took part. Would you have a direct reply to that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a single instance in that war that I was ever in command anywhere. I never even had occasion to have effective command, nor did I have a legal position that would put me in command, nor was I there in the first place when those things happened that we can read about in your indictment. That happened about 20 days after I left Western Slavonia, and it happened in a chaotic situation during the Serb exodus before greatly overpowering Croatian forces. As to the scale of the crime, you can make a judgement only if you compare the number of civilians on the Croat side who were killed with the number of Serb civilians killed during Serbian withdrawal and Croatian conquest of Western Slavonia. I tell you that there are many more Serb victims, but the Office of the Prosecutor here is not interested in hearing it. They didn't prosecute a single Croat for the crimes in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they didn't prosecute anything for the greatest ethnic cleansing of all, the Storm operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's absurd to think that he doesn't know that what he is doing is contrary to your rules, and the time may come when I will invite the Chamber yet again to ask itself the question whether conscious, repeated disobedience of your rules doesn't invoke reconsideration of the use of assigned counsel. He wants to be his own advocate; he ought to behave like one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem with the interpretation. I do have a problem with the interpretation. Please. There occurred a problem. I don't know what "opetovano" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what it means either if indeed it were used. Mr. Milosevic, comments are not allowed. You waste the time of the Court in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. Can I help with the question that you raised earlier about the drafting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And given the author of the document, of which I, of course, happily accept general responsibility, it would be surprising if there wasn't a precise and perfectly conceived reason for the drafting in the form that you find. And indeed, if the Chamber is good enough to go back to paragraph 6 of the Croatian indictment, you will see that the terminology used is very precisely explained there, where it sets out the characteristics of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, and then it says in the second half of the paragraph: "These areas included those regions that were referred to by Serb authorities and are hereinafter referred to as..." and then it sets out the various titles. And so therefore, the adoption for the rest of the indictment of the phrase "Dubrovnik Republic" was simply a use by the drafter of the terminology used by the Serb authorities. Since the Court raised the issue, we have been trying to identify, perhaps to assist you, the particular document or one of the particular documents that may have been in mind at that particular time, and there certainly was, amongst other documents, a document produced in the evidence of Paponjak which may be one of those that was in mind. The Court will have in mind, of course, that Dubrovnik Republic is, from the evidence of this witness himself, a concept well known and regularly used. 14

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it only in paragraph 77?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is only in that paragraph, 77?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't say whether it appears in any other intervening paragraphs, but its use in paragraph 77 was foreshadowed and explained in the paragraph that I've just read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If in other paragraphs you mainly refer to Dubrovnik, I wonder whether there is not some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think in other areas you refer to the district of Dubrovnik or simply Dubrovnik or the city of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: City of Dubrovnik of course might have a particular meaning, referring to the walled and ancient city as opposed to the broader area contemplated by the phrase "Dubrovnik Republic" or if the phrase "area of Dubrovnik" was used, to that term as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. It's in paragraph 67 again. We'll have a look at it. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break, a few words about what Mr. Nice said. He just said that the term "Dubrovacka Republika," the Dubrovnik Republic, is something he uses -- he took over from the terminology of the Serbian authorities. The term Dubrovnik Republic was not used in any terminology of the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I should have said it was Poljanic, not Paponjak. It was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who was the mayor of Dubrovnik. We dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, if you recall, when I put questions in connection with the testimony of Dulovic and Anastasijevic, Mr. Seselj pointed out that he had submitted certain submissions. My collaborators have made copies here. It says number 55 -- submission number 55 and number 56 to the Prosecution. These submissions refer to these two witnesses. Both submissions were made on the 24th of November, 2004; almost a year ago. I don't have the translations here, but I assume, as they were handed in over a year ago, that the other side has in the meantime obtained translations. I wish to put a few questions in connection with these to Mr. Seselj, and I tender both these submissions as exhibits because they contain numerous arguments impeaching the testimony of these two witnesses that Mr. Nice called. Could the liaison officer give Mr. Seselj copies. My collaborators have made 15 copies of these documents, both of them, the submissions by Mr. Seselj. It says this was submitted to the OTP, Ms. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, Ulrich Mussemeyer, Daniel Saxon, and in both cases this -- the date was the 24th of November, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, have you received the copies?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be kind enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has not yet received them. Mr. Milosevic, let me hear again exactly what it is that you intend to do with these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To put it in a nutshell, Mr. Robinson, I wish to tender them as exhibits. Yesterday, if you recall, on several occasions I quoted the statements made by these witnesses or, rather, their testimonies, and Mr. Seselj mentioned that he had made submissions. He --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I have been told by the interpreters to read this to more slowly. The title is "Notice to the accused in this case -- by the accused Mr. Seselj that he intends to present a separate Defence in accordance with Rule 67(A) and (B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence." These are two witnesses who made many claims in the course of their testimony here, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do these documents relate exclusively to these two witnesses or do they cover other matters and other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm able to understand, they relate to these two witnesses. However, they mention many other aspects of these matters. They talk about the Vreme magazine and its role and so on and so forth. However, tendering these two documents would save time, because it would make it possible for me to refrain from asking Mr. Seselj many questions in connection with these two witnesses. He has made written submission in connection with the testimony of these two witnesses, so it would save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We would object to the production of these documents to this Court. If they are produced, then I'll have some very specific questions to ask of the witness about the whole purpose of their original production, but I'd rather not go into that now. It's sufficient to observe at this stage that these documents constitute argument by this witness about two other potential witnesses in his case and two existing witnesses in our case. Insofar as he can give evidence of fact about those witnesses who have given evidence in this case, of course that's acceptable. It can't be rejected, couldn't possibly be argued against. But insofar as he's putting together a document, or has put together and now through this accused seeks to lay before you documents of argument about the value of other witnesses, it should be rejected. It's opening the door far too wide to categories of material that shouldn't be before you. It may be you'll need to have a look at the documents a little bit more to see their general nature, but in summary that's what they constitute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it relates to evidence that they have given in there case, wouldn't it be relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, a written comment by a witness, saying -- coming in, that means that any witness is going to be allowed to present to you, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or might be allowed to present to you his own written arguments on why you should reject other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may not just be comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said insofar as he can give evidence of fact about the witnesses, fine. Let him give the evidence if it's material, if he hasn't already done so. Insofar as it's comment and argument, it's quite wrong for the Chamber to allow witnesses to bring in through an accused's application their own written arguments about existing witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It looks almost like a Rule 89(F) application to my eyes that is being made but without actually technically following the procedure of Rule 89(F). That's what it looks like. Aside of Rule 89(F), as documents themselves, I can't provide any argument in line with the Trial Chamber's recent decisions in relation to the admissibility of documents. A decision we had very recently on Jasovic, the earlier decisions we've had in March and April of this year that cause them to be justified as exhibits in relation to production by a witness of exhibits. But as a result 89(F) statement, if it was to be within that procedure, then of course it is capable of being admissible by that means rather than any other means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, part of the difficulty I have is not knowing what the contents are. One would have to discern the contents. Some of it may be matters of fact. Some of it may be comment. But you're saying irrespective of that it might fall under -- it would follow under Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is capable, if the procedure was followed as outlined by the Appeals Chamber of Rule 89(F), it is capable of coming within that class of documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is here to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We haven't followed the rules of the procedure according to the decision of the Appeals Chamber, but it falls still to be -- to arise under that. The rules of the Appeals Chamber were that they be served on the Prosecution in advance, the witness be called, he confirm his statement, and then the witness be tendered for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. We'll consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, when did you receive a copy of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Two minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your submission is not based on an analysis of the contents of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've been able to read it very, very quickly and see what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as quickly as I have, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you reach a decision, I wanted to point out a few other facts to you. This is without doubt part of the testimony of Mr. Seselj about these witnesses. Secondly, as to what Mr. Kay said, that it should be submitted to the other side is closed, it was submitted to them on the 24th of November, 2004. And furthermore, there is no obstacle to Mr. Nice cross-examining on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But not submitted to them in 2004 for the purposes of this case. And is there anything in it, Mr. Milosevic, that is anything more than argument, argument and comment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there is. I'll put a question to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is there in these documents as regards facts apart from comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. Don't put -- you're making your submissions to us now. If we need the witness, we'll ask him to -- we'll ask him to comment, but at this stage we're concerned with your legal submissions for the admission of these documents, and I have asked you if there is anything in it that is more than comment and argument. If it is only argument and comment, I'm not going to admit it. I will not admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kay, the problem I have with this is that this is not a submission submitted by a witness for -- as his statement. This is an argument of a party. So what is your observation on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You could still -- Your Honour is quite right in relation to what it is and what its content is, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the problem is probative value it has, whether it has any probative value as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Unless it was put in a form for Rule 89(F), which is a -- because there are facts in there in the sense of what this witness was able to see or what he read and what he concluded from what he read, so what his state of mind was. It hasn't been perhaps drafted in a way that Rule 89(F) would generally recognise such a statement. So perhaps it could come within that procedure, but it has not been brought within that procedure, and I can't see any point which I could improve upon the observation Your Honour made about it containing argument. It plainly is argument within his case. It hasn't been prepared as a Rule 89(F) statement for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you haven't said anything so far to convince us that this is a statement of a witness, that it is anything other than the argument, the comments of this witness on two other witnesses in his case. Can you point us to anything that is of a factual nature in these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is of a factual nature is, inter alia, what Mr. Seselj spoke about yesterday, that these are witnesses who wrote about events in Eastern Slavonia and Vukovar in one way up to a certain point in time, he even mentioned the year 1995, and then after 1995 wrote in a completely different way. And this is a comparison between what they wrote at that time and what they testified to here. I hope Mr. Seselj can assist me. He even refers to the testimony of one of them before a Special Court in Belgrade. So these are facts, not just arguments and comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber's ruling is that we will not admit these documents. They are not statements of the witness. They're arguments prepared by him in relation to two other witnesses in his own case. However, Mr. Milosevic, we will allow you to put to the witness questions relating to matters of fact that arise, that are mentioned in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in this document, in your motion of the 24th of November - number 55, that is - you gave certain quotations. For example, on page 31, paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they have not received the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters haven't received the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They will receive copies straight away. What is stated here are facts, Mr. Robinson, facts that pertain to Ovcara and assertions made by a witness here, a witness who testified here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, do you need the statement? Do you need this document in order to put that question to the witness? How does the document assist?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the document assists because it practically disqualifies these two witnesses, showing how contradictory their writings were when compared to their statements made here. And to what extent can any serious person rely on the allegations made by them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is here to give the evidence. He can give it in answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I wanted to do, Mr. Robinson, was to save time, not to go through these documents at all. Since this was copied from a book, one has 100 pages. So that's about 200 pages of your transcript. That's as long as it would be. The other one is half as long. It's very voluminous material. There are many questions contained in it. We could spend an entire day asking him about these things. With the best of intentions of saving time, I wanted to have this exhibited and leave Mr. Nice time to put any kind of questions he wishes to in his cross-examination. Of course, that is up to him entirely. I cannot affect him in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have passed that now because we have ruled we are not admitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is an initial problem identified by the very first question that the accused has asked, and I think that, although I'm leaving it to the Chamber, of course, to decide whether and to what extent the document itself may or may not be used by the accused and the witness in this part of the evidence, if the Court goes, for the purposes of argument, to the larger document page 7, I think we'll find the passage that the accused has it in mind to take the witness to, and he's there setting out - I think this is the paragraph probably - "Anastasijevic wrote," and then there's set out presumably something from a newspaper article. If it's intended to get before you the contents of newspaper articles written by Anastasijevic or the other witness, then what you need is copies of those articles. That should have been provided.
