That's what should have been the evidence. And having it secondhand and through oral testimony is entirely unsatisfactory and makes the process of cross-examination even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us hear the question you're putting. And the English page number, with Mr. Nice's help, is page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, on page 31 here, you quote Anastasijevic, his text, and it says: "The cameras of television reporters filmed a stout officer with a large moustache threatening a scrawny fair-haired representative of the International Red Cross, saying he would throw him into the Vuka river if he persists --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am bamboozled at the moment by the form of procedure that's being adopted here. This document is not admitted. I don't have it in front of me. If you've got questions about matters that Mr. Seselj can deal with from his own direct experience, then they have to be put as questions, not as quotations from you. I just don't follow what's happening here. This is an attempt to use one witness to express views and argument about the evidence given by other witnesses in this case, and I find that a process that is not appropriate. It's a matter for argument at the end of the trial. It's not a matter of evidence, the way it's being conducted at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is not the kind of question that you can ask. This doesn't relate to an issue of fact within the knowledge of the witness. It's not the kind of use that the Chamber is permitting you to make of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber, by majority, will not allow that question to be put. Mr. Milosevic, as I said, you may put to the witness questions of fact within his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, yesterday I quoted the original transcript to you. I quoted several statements. I cannot mention all of them now, but you will recall that. Several statements made by witnesses Dulovic and Anastasijevic in these proceedings, and you fully refuted that. By refuting their statements, you indicated certain motions that you sent to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the other side in relation to those particular witnesses. Did you base these motions on some facts that have to do with these proceedings or did you just give your comments and opinions about these witnesses in these submissions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presented facts, first and foremost, in these motions and only then comments. Motions -- the motions were actually written by the expert team that is there to assist my Defence. They submitted that to me on the basis of their own thorough investigations. Their investigations involved three aspects; testimony in court proceedings, newspaper articles written both by Dulovic and Anastasijevic, and official police information about their behaviour in the relevant period. Here in these motions there was something that was indicated very emphatically, namely the differences between what Jovan Dulovic wrote in Ekspres Politika while the war was going on and the operations that he wrote about, especially the operations in the liberation of Vukovar and his later writings in Vreme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think we are being helped by that. Mr. Milosevic, if you have specific questions which fall within the ambit that I have indicated, then you may put them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the main differences that you indicate in these motions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an enormous number of differences in the way in which events were presented during the war and a few years after the war. Also, in Dulovic's case there are enormous differences in terms of what he said in his testimony and the proceedings against you in this Tribunal as compared to his testimony in the Special Court in Belgrade where the group of indictees related to the Ovcara crime is being tried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the main differences are in terms of what he said here and what he said in his testimony before the Special Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he hear the evidence of the Special Court? Was he there himself? Have efforts been made to produce to this Court the records?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if witnesses make contradictory statements, then the easy and simple way of establishing that is to produce the transcripts of what they've said on two different occasions, not to lead evidence which sounds at the moment like it's hearsay twice removed from the event. Now, this could be -- this could easily be done in writing and save a lot of time if you gathered the material together. You've got all the information you need from getting hold of the two motions that have been referred to, but it's not going to help us to hear hearsay twice removed about events in two different sets of proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, Mr. Seselj has just explained what his team did, and the list is here at the very end. It is a very -- it is a team consisting of many members and also they are highly qualified and competent. This is a matter of public record as well, the transcripts of the Special Court in Belgrade and also the transcripts of the Tribunal here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a fact, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's why, that's why it's a simple exercise for you to do it properly and we should insist on you doing it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is an area in which you could have benefited from advice from assigned counsel. I perceive that this could be a matter of some importance to your case, but the way in which it is being handled makes it very difficult for the Chamber to hear it. If you want to show inconsistencies between the evidence given by these two witnesses in a court in Serbia and the evidence that they have given here in this case, that may very well go to their credibility, but how can you possibly do it through this witness? How can we be assisted? You have had enough experience here to know that the way to do that is to present a transcript of the testimony from the two cases. We can have access to the transcript of the evidence here, but we would certainly need to have access to the transcript in the -- of their evidence in the Special Court as well, and that would make your case much stronger as distinct from merely relying on this witness's recollection of what was told to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this witness has just done what you said should be done. He compared the two in order to see how reliable their statements are. I really have nothing to defend myself as far as Vukovar is concerned here. I wish to have the truth established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we do not before us the prior testimony of the two witnesses in the Special Court, which is the point of the comparison.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Seselj yesterday, in response to a question I put, said that he submitted these motions to the other side and that they contain many important points in order to ascertain how unreliable the testimony of these witnesses is. So if he mentioned that yesterday, I imagine I'm within my rights to ask why he mentioned this, what he mentioned, and what the main elements of these motions are. He mentioned that during his own testimony. I did not plan in advance to submit these motions. He mentioned them. However, since I consider them to be relevant, I'm asking the witness what they contain, and I think that that is very logical. When a witness mentions a particular fact, you have the right to put subquestions to him related to what he himself mentioned. So I'm asking him what these contradictions are indicating that these two witnesses are totally unreliable. Now, you're not letting him answer those questions, but that is your own affair. I'm just indicating that that is my perfectly legitimate right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have been considering the matter because it is an important one. It's important to your case, but the way you have managed it, the way you have presented it is not going to be of assistance. If we were to hear Mr. Seselj give evidence of the discrepancies between the evidence given by those two witnesses here and their evidence given in the Special Court merely on the basis of an analysis done by others, an analysis not done by himself but by others, it would be of very little weight, very little weight. So it's not going to advance your case. What you should do, and I tell you this because it could be vitally important to your case because the discrepancies may be of such a nature that they totally discredit the witnesses, you should get the transcript of the evidence from the Special Court as well as the newspaper writings and present them to us. And as I said, it may very well serve to discredit the witnesses. But doing it through this witness is of very little assistance, because that evidence -- to that evidence we will not be able to attach much weight, even if theoretically, and I can put it no higher than that, the evidence may be admissible as hearsay, it's not the kind of evidence to which we would be able to attach great weight. So this goes to the management of your case, and I am prepared to allow you some time to get the transcript of the -- those two witnesses' evidence in the Special Court and to bring to us evidence, not necessarily through this witness, it could be through another witness, as to the discrepancies. And the discrepancies may be of such a nature that they discredit those witnesses. And that's why I have paid so much attention to it, because these are matters that could serve to strengthen your case. 21 Do you understand what I've said, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, Mr. Robinson. You were very clear. You're asking me to do something that Mr. Seselj has already done, that is to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Let me correct you. He has not done what I just said to you. We do not have the transcript of the evidence from the Special Court here. What Mr. Seselj will be giving is second- or thirdhand hearsay evidence of an analysis done by his experts. And as I said, we will not be able to attach much weight to evidence of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson. I understand that Mr. Seselj cannot answer these questions now because you do not allow it. But he had occasion yesterday to respond to many allegations made by these witnesses, and he refuted them completely. I really have no intention to deal with all the witnesses that Mr. Nice tried to use to corroborate his unprovable allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, bear in mind what I have said. You have assigned counsel, but you do not make use of them. Nonetheless, the Chamber has a duty to assist you since you are, in that sense, virtually unrepresented. You're representing yourself, and it is a duty of the Court to assist you. That is how it is in the jurisdiction from which I come where an accused represents himself. So bear in mind what I have told you. You can get the transcript of the evidence of these two witnesses from the Special Court, and you can, through an appropriate witness, put it to them so that the Chamber may be alerted to discrepancies and discrepancies of such a nature that their credibility could be affected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I simply reinforce what has been said and make one individual comment, which is this: That I, speaking for myself, consider the evidence presented in this way to be inadmissible because it has no probative value. I could not consider the evidence presented in this way to be reliable when there's a perfectly simple, straightforward way of producing the actual material which can be directly compared by the Trial Chamber or through the evidence of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we stopped at paragraph 49 of the Croatian indictment. It's on page 12. I hope you can locate it. It says "Vukovar Hospital." It all relates to that event in Ovcara. Tell me, do you know anything about these events and is it correct what's written here?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know something about these events because I made efforts to find out, but I'm not an eyewitness. And what I found out is rather reliable, namely that the authorities of the Autonomous District of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem asked the JNA that some prisoners from the Vukovar Hospital be turned over to them, with a demand that they be tried for the crimes that they had previously committed over the civilian population of Vukovar. And the information I got is that a certain number, I don't know exactly how many, of those prisoners were turned over to them, after which the prisoners were taken to the farm called Ovcara whereupon the execution of those prisoners occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From all that you managed to find out, who was involved? Was the JNA involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, not a single officer of the JNA was involved, and from what I learned it was some locals who did it who had some outstanding accounts with the prisoners. But I have no direct knowledge about it because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we will not delve into this any deeper because you don't know any more about it than was available from media reports at the time.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dealt with it because it was one of the charges in my indictment. So I had to research it extensively, and my experts are working on it, and the knowledge I have was obtained actually by my experts. What I know firsthand is that at the time of the execution, the commander of the Guards Brigade was not in Vukovar, but General Aleksandar Vasiljevic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by "firsthand," Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned from people who were there, that is reliable information that I got, because I dealt with this question, in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked to a large number of people. I talked in particular to the commander of the Leva Supoderica unit, Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni. I couldn't even tell you the names of all the people with whom I discussed it. Just after the event happened, several months after the event, I made intensive efforts to find out if by any chance some volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party was involved. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Milosevic. We'll hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you see, Mr. Seselj, precisely this witness Jovan Dulovic, whom we mentioned before, mentioned on page 11669 that your men, your drunken men, killed people from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm doing here. I'm analysing. While the fighting for Vukovar was going on, Jovan Dulovic had only praise for the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, and he quoted my statements in his reports, namely that I insist on discipline, on sobriety, and several years later he comes up with totally opposite claims in his writings. He praises Major Jovan Radic as an honourable and honest officer at the time, whereas several years later he invokes his allegedly contemporaneous diary and says that Major Radic was involved in crimes. These are incredible things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, where can we see these writings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, you can see that from transcripts. Second, from newspaper articles, and you can address yourself to the state security service of Serbia, which is now called Security and Documentation Agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Things that were said at the time which were praise for you or praise for your volunteers, you said, "He quoted my statements in his reports, namely that I insist on discipline, on sobriety, and several years later he comes up with totally opposite claims in his writings." Now, what we should be seeing is a report on the one hand, and a writing on the other hand so that we can see the difference. Now, are these available? Can Mr. Milosevic get them and present them to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, it's a very big job. That job was done for me by my experts, and this analysis is their work product, a result of their work. They quote the newspaper, the article, the number of the issue, and the date. But I finance my own experts, and I owe them already a lot of money in arrears for their work. I cannot incur additional expense myself to do something that I have already had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As you know, I did not ask that question. I asked you how Mr. Milosevic could get his hands on the material. You've dealt with the writings, and it must be clear to him that the considerable legal assistance he has will be able to obtain these materials. What about the reports that you quoted? "He quoted my statements in his reports." Who were these reports made to and where can they be found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dulovic, in the paper Ekspres Politika of 1991, quotes how much I insisted that there should be no looters or alcoholics among the fighters and that they should not cause any incidents. He is quoting my words spoken in Vukovar. This same newspaper in which he wrote quotes my call to the Ustasha, asking then to surrender so that the conflict can be resolved peacefully, which I made on Radio Vukovar. The paper Ekspres Politika quoted my statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are all newspaper reports, and again they can be obtained and no doubt you can give the dates of these to Mr. Milosevic, you can pass them to his assistants and obtain the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, as soon as I started testifying in Mr. Milosevic's case I have been prevented from meeting him, and I can say nothing to him apart from what I say in the courtroom. I have no contact with his advisors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's not play games here. You can write down the details. You can pass them to him. You can ask your advisors to do that. There's no problem about giving him basic information to enable him to locate evidence for the production of that evidence in the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this basic information is contained in the submissions that I gave to the OTP as my special defence. It quotes the papers, issues, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies it all. He has all the information he needs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, when you say that everything is contained in these submissions that I'm not allowed to put questions to you about, does this refer what it says on page 51, where you say that Dulovic in his text in Ekspres Politika of the 25th of November, which is certainly later than the 21st of November, does not mention any crimes? However, later on he says that Captain Radic committed crimes. Here he not only does not criticise or accuse him but he praises him.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, I just said that here a little while ago. This is just one example. He was full of praise for Captain Radic, putting him on a pedestal, and later on he accuses him of crimes. He refers to his so-called contemporaneous entries in a diary whereas I prove here these were written later on on orders from others, and this is what I say in my submissions, inter alia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Seselj. I hope we shall be able to go into this in greater detail, but what he says in the original transcript from his testimony here on the 16th of October, 2002, on page 11669, he says that your men, while drunk, killed the people from Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here I prove that he's lying, because I demonstrate what he said about the volunteers in 1991. And he says quite the opposite in the proceedings against you as an OTP witness. And then I go on to demonstrate the contradictions between his testimony in The Hague and his testimony in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dulovic, in the original transcript on page 11668 of the 16th of October, 2002, stated that it was this person nicknamed Kameni, whom we mentioned, who told him about the killing of Croats from the Vukovar Hospital, how they were taken to the Ovcara farm and then on from the farm toward Grabova, where 250 people were killed. He describes him here as a member of your units. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already clarified who Kameni is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the transcript of Dulovic's testimony in the proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe he discussed this with Kameni at all. He's inventing this conversation. Kameni was not among those who shot the prisoners in Ovcara. I know that for certain, and I can guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then he couldn't have told him about something where he was not present.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly he couldn't have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have the page reference here.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although Dulovic himself, as far as I can understand from the transcript, doesn't claim that Kameni participated in the shooting. He remembers the name of Kameni so he says it was Kameni who told him what happened. The story is very naive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you charged in your indictment with the fact that the so-called Seselj's men were in the volunteer units who, from the group of prisoners held in Velepromet, separated off certain people and killed them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is mentioned in the indictment although it has nothing to do with the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party and me personally. You see, for a full two years I have been insisting that the OTP interview me. My only condition is that this should be attended by my legal advisors and videoed. For a full two and a half years, the OTP has been avoiding any conversation with me. My goal, however, is to set out my arguments and evidence ahead of time in order to save time, because it would eliminate certain issues. However, the OTP is avoiding having an interview with me. That is why I have been writing these submissions, putting forward my special defence. I am advising the OTP of what I have at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am stopping you. Much of what you have just said is not relevant. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in the document concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina, you will see that in paragraph 6 there is mention of some sort of plan to remove non-Serbs from a large part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I'm asking you now, did anyone from the government of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to the best of your knowledge, have any kind of plan or goal of removing non-Serbs? It says here from a large -- from large areas of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but my question is from any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one from either the government of Serbia either had such a plan or such an intention. The government in Serbia did everything possible to avoid conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to reach an agreement with the leadership of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian federal unit regarding the future of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, as you have been quite clear about the standpoint of the government of Serbia and the SFRY, did anyone from Republika Srpska have any plan to remove the Muslim population from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The leadership of Republika Srpska had no such plan. To the best of my knowledge, the leadership of Republika Srpska did everything possible to keep the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia, and they insisted on this. The leadership of Republika Srpska, only when it was outvoted in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in a counter-constitutional manner, because a decision of that nature could not be reached by outvoting, it had to be reached by a consensus of all three constituent nations, it was only then that all the deputies of the Serb Democratic Party walked out of the Assembly and organised the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So every subsequent move of theirs was a response to the previous move of the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The more evident their separatist moves became, the more the moves that the Serbs made in response led to the separation of these areas from the control of the executive government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, after this, did the leadership of Republika Srpska have any plan to expel the Muslims? I want to avoid putting a leading question.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The leadership of Republika Srpska, to the best of my knowledge, never had a plan to expel the Muslims. Of course, quite naturally they wanted to have control over as much of Bosnia and Herzegovina as possible, but I'm telling you a very telling fact: In the Serbian army, there was a considerable number of soldiers who were Muslims. For example, in Semberija a considerable number of Muslim men joined the Serb army. These were Muslims whose orientation was towards preserving Yugoslavia, whose interests were very close to the Serb national interests. In Semberija there was a considerable number of Muslims who were soldiers in the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in Semberija there was even a brigade -- a Muslim Brigade in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with these allegations that such an intention existed, I asked you whether there was such a plan in Republika Srpska, and I showed to you a document which has already been admitted in evidence, and that is Karadzic's order of the 19th of August, 1992, which contradicts this, because it orders the prevention of forcible deportation and removal of the population. You read this document here, and you testified that this was the practice at the time.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a number of meetings with the leadership of Republika Srpska; Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Aleksa Buha, and others. And according to my direct information, the leadership of Republika Srpska never had a plan or an intention of expelling the Muslims from the territory of Republika Srpska. Their policy was that if the Muslims wanted to leave, they should not be forced to stay. They should not be treated in the way that Izetbegovic's government was behaving, forcibly detaining the Serbs and preventing them from leaving the territory under Muslim control. This was an essential difference between the two leaderships. However, there were individual incidents where Muslims were persecuted, and I testified to some such cases that I knew about. However, these cases occurred without the knowledge and outside the control of the Serbian leadership in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I won't repeat in connection with these paragraphs from the Bosnian indictment what I have already asked you in connection with the same paragraphs in the Croatian indictment, but I draw your attention to the fact that just as in paragraph 22 of the Croatian indictment, in paragraph 22 of the Bosnian indictment there is an almost Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. identical text in which you are mentioned as a participant in this joint criminal enterprise. As you have already answered questions about the almost identical paragraph in the Croatian indictment which also bears the number 22, please tell me, have you anything to add to what you said about this paragraph now referring to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the period that this indictment relates to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is stated here is absolute nonsense. I did not spread inter-ethnic hatred. My attitude toward the Muslims was always brotherly, friendly. I publicly attacked only pan-Islamists, and that this is the case can be seen from the pre-trial submission of the OTP in my case. They say that I threatened pan-Islamists. I started my political debate with these pan-Islamists ten years before the war began, and all my attacks were against these fundamentalists, these pan-Islamists who are a great evil not only in the Balkans but in the whole world. My attitude towards Muslims as such has always been brotherly and friendly. And the Trial Chamber can see the pre-trial brief of the OTP in my case, which contradicts what is stated in the indictment against you when it comes to me and my role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. In paragraphs 23 and 24 of the Bosnian indictment, it says that -- that's 23. It says: "From 1987 -" and I emphasise 1987, if you can find this paragraph - "until late 2000, Slobodan Milosevic was the dominant political figure in Serbia and the SFRY/FRY. He acquired control of all facets of the Serbian government, including the police and the state security services. In addition, he gained control over the political leaderships of Kosovo, Vojvodina, and Montenegro." Kosovo and Vojvodina I assume are parts of Serbia. Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no dispute here. Kosovo and Vojvodina are integral parts of Serbia. And I wouldn't say that you were the dominant political figure. You were the leading political figure, you were the president of the ruling party and the president of the Republic of Serbia. So you were the political figure number 1 in Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you now, did I gain control over Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was impossible for you to gain control over Montenegro. The then Montenegrin leadership comprised of Momir Bulatovic, Milo Djukanovic and others came to power in Montenegro by declaring themselves publicly to hold political standpoints close to yours, but that was only when they came to power. Afterwards they waged their own independent policy and I know of a whole series of political conflicts between you and them. First of all, in 1991, you parted ways publicly as regards your political orientation. I'm referring to you and Momir Bulatovic, and that was in October. I think it must have been The Hague Conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, The Hague Conference.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the mediation of the European Union concerning Yugoslavia. After this, on his return to the country, Momir Bulatovic faced enormous resistance from his own citizens, and he began changing his position. You were unable to persuade him to change his position, the one he expressed in The Hague, but his own citizens convinced him on his return. So he did begin to change it. I know there were -- there were differences, enormous differences when the constitution of Yugoslavia was being drawn up. Two commissions met, I think in Zabljak on Mount Durmitor in Montenegro, to draw up the draft constitution, and they had verbal clashes. However, compromises were reached and the constitution was drafted and adopted. In 1992, there were conflicts, because at one point in time the Socialist Party to which you belonged in Serbia was opposed to Milan Panic's government. But the Montenegrin leadership supported Milan Panic until the last moment. And when Dobrica Cosic was replaced in 1993 on the initiative of a group of deputies from the Serb Radical Party which was joined by the Socialist Party of Serbia, all the parties from Montenegro voted against his replacement. However, we Serb radicals had our deputies from Montenegro as well, both in the Council of Citizens and the Council of Republics; in both houses of the Assembly. And thanks to the deputies of the Serb Radical Party from Montenegro, the replacement of Dobrica Cosic succeeded. And this is a well-known fact. It's common knowledge in Serbia and Montenegro and very easy to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, thank you. It's time for the adjournment. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in paragraph 24 of the Bosnian indictment, it says: "In his capacity as the President of Serbia and through his leading position in the Socialist Party of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic exercised effective control or substantial influence," et cetera, et cetera. And then that list is mentioned once again that we've already looked at, the members of the joint criminal enterprise. Now, tell me, please, either as president of Serbia or as president of the Socialist Party of Serbia, what kind of control was it that I exercised, for example, over Branko Kostic, Veljko Kadijevic, Milan Babic, Milan Martic, Goran Hadzic, Momir Bulatovic, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, Zeljko Raznjatovic? First of all, any one of the persons I've read now from this list contained in paragraph 24, was any one of these persons a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia or were they part of any government agency in Serbia and I was president of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I remind you, Mr. Milosevic, that at that time you were not president of the Socialist Party of Serbia at all. It was Borisav Jovic who was president of the party. Secondly, none of these persons was a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia, and none of them could be under your control. From a party point of view, you could have been under the control of Borisav Jovic. However, you were political figure number one in Serbia, so I doubt that you could have been under his control, speaking realistically. Branko Kostic came to the federal Presidency from Montenegro. If he could have been under anyone's control, it could have been only the leadership of Montenegro. As for these other persons, it is very difficult to imagine that anyone could have controlled them then. These JNA generals, actually starting from 1991, did not even have the control of the Presidency of Yugoslavia above them. When Zdravko Mustac left Belgrade, Arkan lost the person who exercised control over him, and from then on he was independent, a freelancer. In a TV duel with me, he said that he was an institution in his own right. And indeed so. He had great power; financial power, power in the underground. He had this Serb Volunteer Guard under his control, and he was a real danger to all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on in paragraph 24, it says: "... influenced the actions of the Federal Presidency of the SFRY and later the FRY, the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs, the JNA, the Yugoslav army and the VRS, as well as Serb paramilitary groups." Since you are familiar with all the events from that time, what kind of control or influence can be spoken of in this context, as far as the federal Presidency is concerned, the paramilitary groups, the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal Presidency had eight members, one from each republican province. Therefore, it was absolutely impossible for you to exercise control over that federal Presidency, nor was it possible for anyone to exercise control over it. When the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established, the first president was Dobrica Cosic. In all fairness, he was elected at your initiative, but soon there was a clash between the two of you. Dobrica Cosic surrounded himself with people either who were either Americans themselves or worked for Americans. The former US Ambassador Scanlon was engaged professionally in his office. People knew for years that Svetozar Stojanovic was a CIA spy, and I said that in public too. As for the army of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic was the commander of that army, and he issued commands on the basis of decisions made by the Supreme Defence Council, and you were one of the three members of the Supreme defence Council. In addition to yourself, that was Momir Bulatovic as president of Montenegro, and Dobrica Cosic was president of the Supreme Military Council -- Defence Council. The army of Republika Srpska was commanded by the commander of the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic. In nominal terms, Radovan Karadzic was Supreme Commander, but according to my reliable information, Ratko Mladic did not listen to a living soul. He very soon got under Karadzic's -- got out of Karadzic's control too. He never listened to anyone's orders, and he was indeed very, very independent. As for these paramilitary groups, we've already looked at that, if I can reiterate it for each and every one of them individually, but you did not exercise control over any one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 25, the ways in which this alleged joint criminal enterprise was carried out, the one that you took part in allegedly as well, the ways are described as follows: 25: "Slobodan Milosevic, acting alone and in concert with other members of the joint criminal enterprise..." and then the ways are mentioned: "(a) he exerted effective --" please bear this in mind, because Mr. Robinson drew your attention to this aspect, effective. "-- effective control over elements of the JNA and the VJ which participated in the planning, preparation, facilitation and execution of the forcible removal of the majority of non-Serbs ... from large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So let me put the following question to you: Do you know that, as you say here -- as they say here, some elements of the JNA and VJ participated in the planning, preparation, facilitation, and forcible removal of the majority of non-Serbs from large areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single element of the JNA or the army of Yugoslavia took part in any preparation, planning, facilitation, or execution of the forcible removal of non-Serbs from any territory or did such a plan exist or were there any preparations or was anything done according to some plan systematically, on orders, et cetera. Secondly, I've already testified on the basis of my very reliable knowledge that you could not have control over the JNA while Veljko Kadijevic was minister of defence and Blagoje Adzic chief of General Staff. You could not have control over the army of Yugoslavia either, because, in addition to the fact that Dobrica Cosic, according to the constitution, commanded that army, Milan Panic, the federal Prime Minister, held the portfolio of defence minister. He was both Prime Minister and defence minister. So there was no way that you could have had access to any of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. A few questions ago you mentioned that you took part in the election of Cosic and Panic, Cosic as president of the republic and Panic as Prime Minister, and you also took part in their removal from office. Tell me, what was the attitude of the two of them towards me and towards the Socialist Party of Serbia, and why were they removed from office, Cosic and Panic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Open hostility was the attitude they had towards you. From day one they positioned themselves as political opponents, and they wanted to remove you from the political scene, and they showed that with increasing openness. Milan Panic was a candidate at the special presidential elections for the President of Serbia in December 1992 as your most serious counter-candidate, and he won about one-third of the total vote. Dobrica Cosic supported Milan Panic against you, and during the election campaign he attacked your Socialist Party and the Serb Radical Party, opting for the so-called Depos. That was a coalition of pro-Western parties that was heavily defeated in the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that period of time up to 1993, you've just described the role that Cosic and Panic had vis-a-vis the army of Yugoslavia. Was there any possibility for me to have any influence over the army of Yugoslavia until that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no possibilities for that. After Dobrica Cosic, a man from your party, Zoran Lilic, was elected president of Yugoslavia; however, the defence minister was from Montenegro, Pavle Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In subparagraph (b) of paragraph 25, it says: "He provided financial, logistical, and political support to the army of Republika Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srpska." And then it says, "These forces subsequently participated in the execution of the joint criminal enterprise through the commission of crimes which are in violation of ..." et cetera, et cetera. Now, Mr. Seselj, please give a very unequivocal answer although you've been giving unequivocal answers all along. There is no doubt that Republika Srpska was supported, but what about the VRS? What kind of support did I and the political authorities in Serbia give them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You in Serbia did not give any support to the VRS. It was the army of Yugoslavia that gave assistance to them as a federal institution at the outset. What was said was that within the overall support and assistance to Republika Srpska, the civilian authorities of Republika Srpska should also be given a particular amount of money that would be used for financing the army of Republika Srpska. Then there were big polemics in Republika Srpska, and the officers of the army of Republika Srpska opposed that, saying that some unconscientious ministers could use that money for other things. For example, they bore in mind the fact that Momcilo Mandic, minister of the interior, was a notorious criminal, as were others. So they sought other ways and means of having this assistance paid more directly. So then the army of Yugoslavia set up a personnel centre whose task was to have that money that had been earmarked as financial assistance be paid out as salaries to officers of the army of Republika Srpska. This personnel centre was well known under a particular number. I cannot say exactly whether it was 20 or 10 or -- it was some kind of a number that was used as its official title.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Seselj, tell us, was the aim of this assistance the execution of a joint criminal enterprise, as is claimed in this piece of paper here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. That's not a permissible question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, what was the aim of providing this assistance? What was the aim and purpose of providing this assistance to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all sides - from the West, from the Arab countries, from the Islamic countries - the Muslim government in Sarajevo was deluged with all the money coming in. Later on a direct armed intervention followed, and in this way it was the Bosnian Croat leadership that was also given assistance from elsewhere. It was simply indispensable to help the Serb people by helping their Republika Srpska, Republika Srpska which was inalienably theirs, undoubtedly theirs, so that they would survive under conditions when their political and military enemies had far more support and financial assistance. This assistance was given to the Government of Republika Srpska. However, one of the concrete aspects of this assistance was the payment of these salaries because, among the officers, it was not a very popular idea to have this assistance channeled to the government too. They were afraid that there would be major delays if this went through the government, that some ministers would engage in speculation as far as this money was concerned, so it was agreed that they would receive this assistance directly. This assistance was never aimed at financing any kind of criminal activities or did the army of Republika Srpska engage in any criminal activity. Crimes were committed during the war. Sometimes the persons who committed these crimes were members of the army of Republika Srpska but this was only in exceptional cases when there were particular incidents but not on orders from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have answered the specific question about the aim and purpose of providing assistance to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Seselj, look at subparagraph (c). It says: "He exercised substantial influence over, and assisted, the political leadership of Republika Srpska in the planning, preparation, facilitation and execution of the takeover of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the subsequent forcible removal of the majority of non-Serbs, principally Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, from those municipalities." Immediately follows subparagraph (d), which reads: "He participated in the planning and preparation of the takeover of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the subsequent forcible removal of the majority of non-Serbs..." and so on. "He provided the financial, material, and logistical support necessary for such takeover." I cannot really make out the difference between subparagraphs (c) and (d). They seem to boil down to the same thing. Would you please answer this question: How did I try to influence the leadership of Republika Srpska? In other words, I tried to influence them to do what, and what was the extent of my influence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even the leadership of Republika Srpska itself was able to control the process of takeover of power in municipalities. According to my information, which is direct and reliable, that process was often uncontrolled and certain measures were often taken against the wishes of the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party or, later, the leadership of Republika Srpska. It began with the establishment of Serbian autonomous districts such as Eastern Herzegovina, Birac, SAO Romanija, SAO Semberija and Majevica, Bosnian Krajina, et cetera. A similar process was taking part with the Croats. They had three such districts; Western Herzegovina, that is Herceg-Bosna; Central Bosnia; and the Croatian Posavina, as they called it. At the moment when the central authorities in Sarajevo with its unilateral steps abolishing the essential right of the peoples to the status of constituent nation, this process was aggravated and accelerated. I'll give you one example: The leadership of the Serbian Autonomous District of Bosnian Krajina not only did not cooperate with the leadership in Pale, together with Milan Babic they unilaterally proclaimed the unification of Bosnian Krajina with the Serbian Krajina in Croatia. So these things happened spontaneously for the most part. It sometimes happened that Serbs seized power in municipalities where they were not a majority population because they organised themselves better than Croats and Muslims did. The latter two also wanted to seize power, but the decisive factor was better organisation, greater quantity of weapons, and the managing abilities of those who led the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us dwell a little on what I just quoted, because both subparagraph (c) and (d) refer to the preparation and execution of the takeover. Did the leadership of Republika Srpska ever plan some sort of forcible removal of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They only wanted to have control over as many municipalities as possible. They wanted, in other words, effective power, but they never wanted Croats or Muslims to be forcibly removed or deported from their territory. Not a single order, not a single command, not a single decision was ever made, to the best of my knowledge, by the central Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're now talking about separate, distinct parts of Republika Srpska, and you mentioned Serbian Krajina, the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Do you know for how long there was no physical communication between the leadership in Pale and the western part, the whole Banja Luka region, until the corridor was made through Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know for how long but for a long time there was no communication at all. It was impossible to travel, there were no telephone lines working, and the Bosnian Krajina was completely isolated from the rest of Republika Srpska. Once the corridor was made, then the unified Serb authorities set about getting established. That's the corridor in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in the end of June.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that time, following the instructions of the leadership that had started to consolidate its power in the western area as well, those camps that had existed in the western area were abolished?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The central authorities made the appropriate decision, demanding that these camps be abolished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed they were by August.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, by August they were all abolished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how they came to be set up at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the three best-known camps of this type were in the area of the municipality of Prijedor, and it was Simo Drljaca who set them up on his own accord. He happened to be the chief of police there. However, when the existence of these camps became known, they were abolished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were all abolished by August?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about these municipalities where it says here that a takeover took place? Did Serbs continue to hold the leading posts in most of the authorities of these municipalities, or were they previously in the highest positions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were mostly Prime Ministers or heading those municipalities. So they just -- they took more power than was actually provided for by the legislation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did the takeover consist in if they were already in power, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was often a matter of conflict between the Muslim leadership and the Serb leadership in the given municipality. It was a race to get hold of complete power over the municipality. The civilian population had already started to arm itself and at a certain point a race began as to who would be the first to gain complete control over the municipality. In those places where Serbs were a majority, it was easier to carry out. Where the Muslims were a majority, it was mainly them who prevailed. In municipalities with the Croat majority, Croats won over, but it sometimes happened that Serbs took over thanks to better organisation and similar advantages. As to the rest of your question, there was no material, financial, or logistical support or help from Serbia. These were mainly spontaneous processes led by the Serbian Democratic Party and financial and material assistance from Serbia was not even needed. In some places a unit of the JNA would be the decisive factor in such a case, because what happened when the war broke out in the federal unit of Croatia, the reservists of the JNA started to be mobilised even in Bosnia. The Muslims initially responded to the call-up, but when their leadership appealed to them not to do so, they stopped. Croats had stopped responding to call-ups even before, and it so happened -- or, rather, so it happened that it was mostly Serbs who responded to the call-up, and thus they had more weapons than both Muslims or Croats. However, the illegal channels of arms supply to both Muslims and Croats also worked very well, so the difference in the level of arming was not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In subparagraph (e), reference is made to the special forces of the Republic of Serbia, but what matters to me more is the second part, which says that these special forces participated in the execution of the joint criminal enterprise through the commission of crimes which are in violation of Articles, and so on and so forth, of the statute. Tell me, did the special forces of the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Internal Affairs take part in any activities within which crimes were committed? You can see it for yourself if you are looking at paragraph 25(e). So special forces participated in the execution of the JCE.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was only one special unit of the Interior Ministry of Serbia at that time. It was the so-called special anti-terrorist unit, acronym SAJ. As far as I know, SAJ was never involved in any fighting outside of Serbia, and in Serbia there was no fighting at all at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. With regard to this Croatian part of the indictment, you have already told us what you knew about special forces. What about Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is there anything that you would like to add to the explanations you've provided before about these special forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is an invitation, that's a very dangerous invitation to Mr. Seselj, would he like to add anything. Be focused in the questions that you're asking. Mr. Seselj, I'm sure, would like to add many, many things. The question is whether they're of assistance to the Chamber in its work. So ask a specific and focused question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I only wanted to save time, because in the Bosnian indictment the qualifications used in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Croatian indictment about the alleged participation of special forces are repeated, and Mr. Seselj has already said what he knew about it. I'm just asking him whether what he said refers or applies to both indictments or whether there is any difference, whether he had anything to add. But the qualifications are completely the same. Even the numbers of subparagraphs are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would just like to say that in the first half of 1992, the Yugoslav People's Army included a certain number of volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party in certain critical areas where they expected their units to be the most threatened. One of such areas was Zvornik. So the JNA engaged volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party exclusively as an addition to its troops, to its regular troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm sorry to interrupt you but it occurs to me that I should you asking you now how much more time will you be with this witness? I had anticipated that you would have completed your examination-in-chief by the end of today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm proceeding a bit slower than I thought I would so I can't finish today, because we've only got 30 minutes left until the end of today. I will not be able to finish by then. I will try to complete this examination before the end of the first working day that follows, Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's Monday. The first -- Monday. The first working day is Monday, Monday afternoon. I believe you have been --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I must have been misinformed, because I thought it would have Tuesday. But whatever the first following working day is, on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Monday afternoon. Well, we're going to hold you to that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Seselj is informed that the first following working day is Monday.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, no. And it is important for me to know, because I scheduled a visit of my family for Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday. Will I be able to have the Monday two weeks from now free so my family can visit me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you talking about Monday two weeks from now? We're talking about Monday --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, at that time we'll be -- it will be time for cross-examination. I'm not able to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not sitting on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not sitting on Monday. We're not sitting that Monday. Give us the date. Monday the 12th. We are not sitting on Monday the 12th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a very direct question: These special forces, and you said already there was one anti-terrorist unit, the equivalent of which existed in every republic within the Interior Ministry, did special forces operate in Bosnia and in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to what I know, no special forces from Serbia participated. Only additional troops of the JNA were sent there. Some other groups and individuals were engaged. Biljana Plavsic, for instance, brought Arkan and his men to Bijeljina. Arkan turned up also in Zvornik, from what I know. Yellow Wasps came to Zvornik on their own initiative. That had nothing to do with the JNA. I can guarantee for that. Maybe another smaller group appeared elsewhere as well, but the legal unit from Serbia was not engaged. No legal unit from Serbia outside the JNA was sent anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were any forces -- when I say "any," I mean regular forces. You're referring to various groups such as the Yellow Wasps who have been tried in Belgrade. So did any regular forces, either of the police or the military, originating from Serbia participate in anything that might be considered to be the implementation of a joint criminal enterprise or a crime?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No forces apart from the JNA, and the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 19th of May, which was the ultimatum given by the Western forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the statements contained in the indictment for Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was the attitude of the authorities of the Republic of Serbia and my own attitude toward irregular and paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always negative. You always demonstrated your efforts to suppress the activity of any paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any cases where the authorities of the Republic of Serbia arrested and tried members of paramilitary troops?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already mentioned the trials of the Yellow Wasps. There were many instances where members of these paramilitary formations, when attempting to cross the border, were stopped, disarmed, searched, and so on. At police checkpoints certain quantities of weapons were discovered in their possession and confiscated by the police. I think at one point the police was able to fill their depots and equip themselves with such weapons, replenish their supplies. If I may add, Mr. Milosevic - I think this is important - the Serbian police set up these checkpoints on all roads leading towards Slavonia and Bosnia. And when the hostilities began, probably because they had experience from 1991, they had checkpoints everywhere and exerted the maximum efforts to make sure that no one from Serbia went to flashpoints outside Serbia. And of course there were attempts on the other side to try to prevent the influx of illegal weapons into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subparagraph (g) is almost identical to the same statement contained in the Croatia indictment. It says that I "controlled, manipulated, or otherwise utilised Serbian state-run media in Serbia to spread exaggerated and false messages of ethnically based attacks by Bosnian Muslims and Croats against Serb people intended to create an atmosphere of fear and hatred among Serbs living in Serbia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina which contributed to the forcible removal of the majority of non-Serbs, principally Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, from large areas of Bosnia on Herzegovina." So mutatis mutandis, the same allegation contained in the Croatian document resurfaces here. Tell me, please, is this correct and to what extent did the Serbian media influence public opinion in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because this refers to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is simply impossible. There was only one state-run media in Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Serbia, interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the RTS, the Serbian Radio and Television. All other television and radio stations were either privately owned or in the hands of local authorities. All the newspapers were privately owned or, rather, owned by joint stock companies or individual private entrepreneurs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In general, because you had a very active political life at the time, speaking generally, the state-run media and these privately owned media, did they spread exaggerated stories of ethnically motivated attacks by Muslims on Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no untrue or exaggerated message. The media conveyed information from the ground. This information was horrifying in its nature, but it was verified and it was true. If this caused unease and if it disturbed the public in Serbia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is those who committed crimes against the Serb people who contributed to this atmosphere, not those who merely conveyed true facts to the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that yesterday you mentioned the first murder that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a result of the tensions that had arisen, and you mentioned the name of Nikola Gardovic, the murder at that wedding you mentioned. I won't go into the details now, but do you know anything about crimes committed against Serbs in the area of Bosanski Brod, to be more precise the village of Sijekovac, in late March 1992 before the outbreak of any kind of -- or before the onset of any kind of activities on the Serb side that might provide some kind of justification?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there was a massacre there of a group of Serb civilians in that village of Sijekovac, if I recall the name correctly. I had it noted down somewhere, but I can't find it now. This was the village of Sijekovac near Bosanski Brod. I think 20 or 21 Serbs were slaughtered, and these were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number was 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hesitate to rise yet again but I suppose I might as well draw to your attention that we are now having evidence really with no identified source. The witness seems to recall something, he can't remember the name; and then when he provides a number that the accused don't like, the accused volunteers an alternative number. I shall make my observations through the witness about the quality of his evidence in due course, but this is both generalised and, in part, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. You will have the occasion to cross-examine the witness. In the meantime, Mr. Milosevic, bear in mind the prohibition of leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in your transcript, which is still on the screen, you can see Mr. Seselj's reply: "This was the village of Sijekovac near Bosanski Brod. I think 20 or 21 Serbs were slaughters, and these were civilians." He says 20 or 21 Serbs were slaughtered, and these were civilians, and I simply said 21. He said 20 or 21 before I said 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall all these figures with precision, but I do remember the crimes in those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You should have left the evidence there, 20 or 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The problem is how he did come to know these facts, so you should lay the foundation of this evidence. That's the point of Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have been through that with you several times before. It doesn't really make the evidence inadmissible, but we will not be able to attach as much weight to it as we would if we knew how he acquired the information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was about to be my next question. I asked him whether he knew about the crimes against the Serbs in Sijekovac. He said he did. He said that 20 or 21 people were killed. Let's put aside the fact that I said 21 because I have the precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: Mr. Seselj, how do you know what happened in the village of Sijekovac near Bosanski Brod in late March 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a well-known fact. It's a notorious crime. It was in all the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your knowledge of this originate exclusively from the media or did you have some knowledge from the ground?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we also had information from the ground. Later on, I travelled to these places, and the local people, of course, remembered this. They cannot forget something like this. This is a fact. The truth of this cannot be relative. It either happened or it did not happen. I tell you it did happen and I have information that it did. The first information arrived through the media. Later on, it was confirmed many times in direct contacts with local people from the area. So there can be no doubt when one is speaking of specific events like this. They either happened or not, but you can't expect me to recall the precise number of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you mentioned Gardovic and the 1st of March, 1992. Now you mentioned Sijekovac on the 26th of March, 1992. In the meantime, even before this, was there any violence on the Serb side against Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me remind you of an even more horrendous crime against Serbs in Posavina in the village of Kostres where more than a hundred Serbs were killed. They were killed by Muslims from a village called Korace or something like that. So this was an even more horrifying crime from that period. It was in early April 1992. And we have more instances like that. In Kupres, a large number of Serbs were killed; over a hundred. These are not isolated incidents. It happened frequently, in many places, and it indicated the intentions of the Muslim political leadership and its paramilitary formations, the Green Berets. That's the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You've mentioned the examples of Sijekovac, the village of Kostres. You said in early April a large number, over a hundred, you said. You mentioned the murder of a large number of people in Kupres.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 50, maybe even a hundred was the number killed in Kupres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. All this marked the beginning of the conflicts, and we can see that dozens and hundreds of Serbs were killed.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In different places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In different places. Up to that time, had the Serbs killed anyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know of no instance of the Serbs killing anyone. It was the Muslims and Croats who did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that time when these mass murders of Serbs began, did the Serbs respond violently in any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Up to that point, no, as far as I know. And by then everything was already clear; either they would defend themselves and save their homes and their hearths or they would all be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these crimes when hundreds of Serbs were slaughtered, did they take place before the recognition of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and some kind of official onset of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened at least two days, this murder in Kostres, at least two days before the recognition of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They knew in the West what was going on and yet they recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this spoiled the Cutileiro Plan which had been adopted. And then independence was recognised and the Muslims simply scuttled it because what did they need the plan for when they already had recognition?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just establish this: Before the recognition of independence, hundreds of Serbs were killed.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And no one was killed by a Serb. There were no violent actions by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assert that emphatically, and my information is reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Seselj. I just wanted to hear your opinion. In the Bosnian indictment, paragraph 26 mentions the Serbian Bloc in the SFRY and Borisav Jovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology: 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Branko Kostic, Jugoslav Kostic, Sejdo Bajramovic, and now it says here that I used them as my mediators, my primary agents, and through them directed the actions of the Serbian Bloc. This paragraph is quite long, so I will ask you to read it for yourself. It's paragraph 28, and it says: "From at least March 1991 until the 15th of June, 1992, Slobodan Milosevic exercised effective control..." and they are listed here and they are referred to as my primary agents in the Presidency. And it says: "From the 1st of October, 1991, in the absence of the representatives of the Presidency from Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, the four members ... exercised the powers of the Presidency ..." So first of all, Mr. Seselj, tell me, how did it come about that these members of the Presidency from Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were absent?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first one to leave was, I think his name was Janez Drnovsek. He was from Slovenia. And then Stipe Mesic and then Bogic Bogicevic from Bosnia and Herzegovina withdrew; after that, Vasil Tupurkovski from Macedonia stopped attending, but the Presidency had a general legal document according to which in conditions of a situation of war and imminent threat of war or a state of emergency, the number of representatives who happened to be in Belgrade could make decisions as if they were all there in these extraordinary circumstances, and this rule or this legislation was in existence. Secondly, these people were not sheep, to be controlled just like that. You cooperated with Borisav Jovic, but he is a strong personality, and you couldn't have commanded him, given him orders. Branko Kostic was the representative of Montenegro. Sejdo Bajramovic was an Albanian but a sincere patriot and an advocate of Yugoslavia. His son was killed in the Mostar war theatre as a JNA officer, fighting the paramilitary formations. Sejdo Bajramovic is a senior cadre. He was a communist, one can hold that against him, but he believed in Yugoslavia to such an extent as an equal community of nations, and he saw the future of his own Albanian nation within it and no one could have influenced him in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here in this paragraph: "This 'Rump Presidency' acted without dissension to execute Slobodan Milosevic's policies." Please, Mr. Seselj, the mentioned members of the Presidency, did they act without dissension to execute my policies, and what do you know about this from that period of time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, there is no such thing as a rump Presidency. According to the constitution, the Presidency was authorised to issue general legal documents regulating its own work and procedure. That was what they did independently. And considerably before the war they adopted a general legal document according to which it could never be a rump Presidency. A member of the Presidency could die, could be taken prisoner by the enemy. For as long as one of them was alive and in Belgrade, he could be the Presidency according to that general legal document which can easily be obtained from Belgrade. It was impossible to have any such thing as a rump Presidency. Secondly, it was also impossible for it to execute your policies without dissension. On the Presidency were people of high personal integrity, people who had their own steadfast political views and a firm desire to preserve Yugoslavia. As for Sejdo Bajramovic, who I knew personally, nobody could influence him to the extent that he would change his own political positions. He was firmly in favour of Yugoslavia. And he did not even regret sacrificing his own son for the future of Yugoslavia. His son died the death of a hero at the Mostar theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of this is lumped together here. "Generals Veljko Kadijevic and Blagoje Adzic, who directed and supervised the JNA forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were in constant communication and consultation with the accused." Can you explain what this means? Can you tell us what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they probably did have that kind of communication with you. I don't know, I was never present. I didn't know you, I didn't know Adzic, I didn't know Kadijevic. However, I read Borisav Jovic's book and I see that this communication was always beset by various problems. You held different positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, The first part of the witness's answer tells us that he doesn't know anything about these people, so how is his answer going to be helpful? But we will break at this point. It's time to adjourn for the day. We will resume on Monday at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of September, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
